title: 3D Trigonometry

findings.finding: The first worked example applies Pythagoras’ theorem without an opening rehearsal of its two-dimensional use.
findings.breakdown: Students must recall how to form the sum of the squared perpendicular lengths and recover the hypotenuse length. The topic identifies the hypotenuse explicitly, so identifying it is not a separate missing review piece.
findings.checked: There is no earlier topic or opening review. p3-definition-method identifies the relevant sides and names Pythagoras, but does not rehearse applying the theorem before p3-example-body.
findings.assumptions: Pythagoras is prior learning. A calculator is assumed; evaluating squares and roots is not itself the missing review skill.

repair.proposal: Before p3-definition-intro, add: (a) A right triangle has perpendicular sides 6 cm and 8 cm. Write a Pythagoras equation for its hypotenuse h. Answer: h²=6²+8². (b) Find h. Answer: 10 cm. (c) A right triangle has perpendicular sides 5 cm and 7 cm. Find its hypotenuse exactly. Answer: √74 cm. Keep the review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: Students rehearse forming and solving a Pythagoras equation before the first 3D example.

findings.finding: p7-q6-b introduces both a pyramid’s interior height triangle and a centre-to-corner base distance without a preceding bridge.
findings.breakdown: Earlier two-stage problems use complete edges and face diagonals. Students must now select an interior section, halve a base diagonal and use subtraction to find the height.
findings.checked: p7-q6-a rehearses finding a shorter side, but not the pyramid construction. The later p7-q7 already bridges this change through a base diagonal, a face midpoint, a face height and the perpendicular height. Its different route still provides the needed preparation for selecting internal pyramid triangles.
findings.assumptions: Ordinary square geometry and Pythagoras are prior knowledge. Calculator use is assumed.

repair.proposal: Move the whole shared-stem p7-q7-root, including its diagram and all parts, immediately before p7-q6-root. Retain its existing questions and answers.

findings.doneWhen: The scaffolded pyramid-height question precedes the independent pyramid calculations in p7-q6.

findings.finding: Extend the cube question by comparing surface area and volume when its space diagonal doubles.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up connects a linear scale change with the resulting area and volume changes.
findings.checked: For space diagonal 40 m, the side is 40/√3 m, surface area is 3200 m² and volume is approximately 12316.8 m³. Relative to the original cube, the factors are 4 and 8.
findings.assumptions: Cube surface area and volume are available methods, as required by the existing question. A calculator is assumed.

repair.proposal: After p8-q9-b, add: (c) A second cube has space diagonal 40 m. Find its surface area to 1 decimal place. Answer: 3200.0 m². (d) Find its volume to 1 decimal place. Answer: 12316.8 m³. (e) How many times the original cube’s surface area is the second cube’s surface area? Answer: 4. (f) How many times the original cube’s volume is the second cube’s volume? Answer: 8.

findings.doneWhen: The numerical follow-up compares the two cubes using the existing question’s methods.

findings.finding: The worked example requires selecting a trigonometric ratio and recovering an angle without opening rehearsal of either skill.
findings.breakdown: Students must connect opposite and adjacent lengths to tangent, then use inverse tangent. The preceding topic practises Pythagoras rather than these trigonometric decisions.
findings.checked: All supplied earlier teaching and practice were checked. Neither ratio selection nor inverse trigonometry is rehearsed before p9-example-body; its worked equations use both.
findings.assumptions: Right-triangle trigonometry is prior learning. A scientific calculator in degree mode is assumed.

repair.proposal: Before p9-information-introduction, add: (a) In a right triangle, θ has opposite side 5 cm and adjacent side 12 cm. Write a trigonometric equation for θ. Answer: tan θ=5/12. (b) Find θ in (a), to the nearest degree. Answer: 23°. (c) In a right triangle, θ has opposite side 6 cm and hypotenuse 10 cm. Find θ to the nearest degree. Answer: sin θ=6/10, θ=37°. Keep the review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: Students rehearse selecting a ratio and using its inverse before the 3D worked example.

findings.finding: Plane-inclination questions require selecting a perpendicular section, but preceding instruction establishes only line-to-base angles.
findings.breakdown: An arbitrary sloping line in a plane need not give the plane’s inclination. Students need to select two lines perpendicular to the planes’ intersection.
findings.checked: The supplied teaching contains no plane-angle rule. In p11-q5 the intersection is BF; BD and BA are perpendicular to BF, so ∠DBA measures the inclination and tan ∠DBA=2/4, giving 27°. The later pyramid and prism questions also require this selection.
findings.assumptions: Prior right-triangle trigonometry does not establish the definition of the angle between planes.

repair.proposal: Prepend scaffolded parts to p11-q5: 'Measure the angle between two planes using a line in each plane perpendicular to their line of intersection.' (a) Name the line where plane DBFH meets the base. Answer: BF. (b) At B, name a line in plane DBFH and a line in the base that are both perpendicular to BF. Answer: BD and BA. (c) Name the angle between the planes. Answer: ∠DBA. Retain the existing calculation.

findings.doneWhen: Students select a perpendicular section in p11-q5 before applying the rule in the later plane-angle questions.

findings.finding: Extend the cube question by comparing space-diagonal inclinations in two sizes of cube.
findings.breakdown: Students connect proportional lengths with an unchanged trigonometric ratio.
findings.checked: A cube of side 4 m has base diagonal 4√2 m and space diagonal 4√3 m. Its inclination is arctan(1/√2), approximately 35.3°, matching the original cube.
findings.assumptions: A scientific calculator in degree mode is assumed. All required methods occur by the end of this topic.

repair.proposal: After p10-q1-c, add: (d) A second cube has side length 4 m. Find its base diagonal exactly. Answer: 4√2 m. (e) Find its space diagonal exactly. Answer: 4√3 m. (f) Find the angle its space diagonal makes with its base, to 1 decimal place. Answer: 35.3°. (g) Explain why this angle equals the angle in part (c). Answer: the perpendicular height and base diagonal both double, leaving their ratio unchanged.

findings.doneWhen: The follow-up compares the two numerical cubes and explains their equal inclinations.

findings.finding: Extend the tower problem by doubling its height while retaining its elevation angles.
findings.breakdown: Students connect fixed elevation angles with proportional ground distances and separation.
findings.checked: With height 300 m, the separation is √((300/tan 28°)²+(300/tan 33°)²)=729.2108… m. Both horizontal legs double, so the exact separation doubles.
findings.assumptions: A scientific calculator in degree mode is assumed. The existing worked example supplies all required methods.

repair.proposal: Append to p13-guided-root: (a) A second tower is 300 m tall. Points X′ and Y′ are due south and due east of it, with elevation angles 28° and 33° respectively. Find X′Y′ to the nearest metre, using unrounded intermediate values. Answer: 729 m. (b) Explain why the exact distance X′Y′ is twice XY. Answer: each horizontal leg is the height divided by the same tangent, so both legs double and Pythagoras gives X′Y′=2XY.

findings.doneWhen: The follow-up calculates the new separation and explains its exact scale relationship.

protectedGroups.observation: A side face and a slant edge of the same pyramid have different inclinations to the base.
protectedGroups.varies: The inclined object and its associated horizontal distance: CM versus CQ.
protectedGroups.invariant: The pyramid, perpendicular height and base.

protectedGroups.observation: The same prism dimensions produce different face diagonals because the relevant face changes.
protectedGroups.varies: Requested face and the pair of perpendicular edge lengths.
protectedGroups.invariant: Prism dimensions, vertex convention and exact-answer method.

protectedGroups.observation: The two-triangle method survives changes of orientation while separate drawing support fades.
protectedGroups.invariant: Find BE exactly, then use it to find BH.

protectedGroups.observation: Comparing calculations with an exact and a rounded shared height reveals the effect of intermediate rounding.
protectedGroups.invariant: The geometry, measurements and final angle being calculated.

protectedGroups.observation: The same spatial distance-and-bearing method survives changes in numerical orientation, support and observation direction.
protectedGroups.varies: Bearings, elevation versus depression, and the amount of scaffolding.
protectedGroups.invariant: Two perpendicular horizontal distances obtained from a common vertical height.

Under the opening-review exception for skills practised in the preceding topic, another rehearsal is not required.

candidates.finding: The example immediately uses “tan35°=100/AC” and “AC=100/tan35°”, but there is no review of choosing tangent or solving a trigonometric equation with the unknown length in the denominator.

supplementalReviews.reason: Close the original image-visibility limitation through a scoped later inspection; the original worker did not see page 21.
supplementalReviews.outcome: Source page 21 and retained student rendered page 32 were visually inspected. Both show vertical TF, ground AB perpendicular AF, 55-degree TAF and 40-degree TBF; current figure makes these relationships readable. No additional pedagogy recommendation: preceding p18-q13 and p20-q18 already express triangle lengths in h and combine them using Pythagoras. Here parts (a) and (b) scaffold the sightline lengths and right angle before the closing derivation.
supplementalReviews.mathematicsChecked: AT=h/sin55°, BT=h/sin40°. AB is horizontal and perpendicular to AF, hence perpendicular to plane AFT and AT. BT²=AT²+50² gives exactly the printed positive expression for h. The denominator is positive since sin55°>sin40°.
